interview.question: What does Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER represent?
interview.answer: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 9007199254740991, or 2^53 − 1. It is the largest integer that a JavaScript Number can represent exactly and compare correctly.
interview.followUp: What can happen above this value? Different integers may round to one Number value, so equality and integer arithmetic can become unreliable; use BigInt for larger integers.

interview.question: Why is the safe-integer limit 2^53 − 1?
interview.answer: JavaScript Numbers use double-precision floating point, whose mantissa provides 53 bits of integer precision. That makes 2^53 − 1 the largest safely distinguishable integer.
interview.followUp: Why does the limit apply to integers rather than all numeric values? Floating-point Numbers can represent much larger magnitudes, but not every integer in those magnitudes exactly.

interview.question: Should all arithmetic above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER be avoided?
interview.answer: The property itself is a Number value, so arithmetic beyond it can still produce meaningful approximate results, but integer-level precision is not guaranteed. For exact large-integer calculations, BigInt is the appropriate alternative.
interview.followUp: Can Number.MAX_VALUE replace it? No: MAX_VALUE is the largest representable Number magnitude, whereas MAX_SAFE_INTEGER concerns exact integer precision.

keyPoints: It is a static data property on Number that identifies JavaScript's upper safe-integer boundary.
Its decimal value is 9,007,199,254,740,991.
The safe integer interval is symmetric, extending from the corresponding negative limit through this positive limit.
Safety means exact representation and correct integer comparisons, not merely that the value is finite.
MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is not JavaScript's largest possible numeric magnitude; Number.MAX_VALUE is larger.
Operations above the boundary are permitted, although they no longer guarantee integer-level precision.
gotchas: Different mathematical integers above the boundary can compare equal after rounding to the same Number value.
Access it on Number, not through an individual numeric value.

Numeric Separators.summary: Numeric separators are underscores placed between digits in a number literal, such as 1_000_000. They improve readability while leaving the represented numeric value unchanged.
Numeric Separators.explanation: Numeric separators let you place underscores between digits in numeric literals. JavaScript ignores those underscores when evaluating the literal, so the value is unchanged; they are only syntactic sugar for readability.

example.title: Readable numeric literals
example.explanation: Underscores make digit groups easier to read while preserving the numeric value.

useCases.title: Grouped non-decimal literals
useCases.scenario: Representing hexadecimal, binary, or other supported numeric literals with grouped digits.

interview.question: What are numeric separators in JavaScript?
interview.answer: Numeric separators are underscores inserted between digits of a numeric literal, such as 1_000_000. The engine ignores them, so the literal has the same value as 1000000.
interview.followUp: Can a separator be used outside a numeric literal? No; this feature is syntax for numeric literals, not a general number-formatting operation.

interview.question: Why use numeric separators?
interview.answer: They improve the readability of large numeric literals without requiring string conversion or runtime formatting. For example, 1_000_000 clearly groups the digits while remaining a number.
interview.followUp: How would you display locale-specific grouping instead? Use number-formatting APIs such as Intl.NumberFormat rather than source-level separators.

interview.question: How is a numeric separator written?
interview.answer: The separator is written as an underscore between digits, as in 1_000_000_000. It is part of the literal’s source syntax and is removed conceptually when the value is interpreted.
interview.followUp: What value does 1_000_000_000 produce? It produces the same number as 1000000000.

keyPoints: An underscore can separate digit groups in a numeric literal.
The syntax works directly in ordinary decimal literals.
The separator is syntactic sugar intended to make source code easier to read.
Grouping digits visually helps readers recognize large quantities.
gotchas: Separators affect source readability only; they do not change the numeric value.

Object key order.summary: JavaScript objects use a special key order: integer property names come first in ascending numeric order, while other string keys follow creation order. Thus, object enumeration is not always simple insertion order.
Object key order.explanation: When JavaScript enumerates an object’s own keys, integer-index-like property names come first in ascending numeric order. Other string keys retain the order in which they were created, so insertion order applies only to that second group.

example.title: Object key enumeration order
example.explanation: Integer-index-like keys are listed first in numeric order; other string keys follow their creation order.

useCases.title: Reading puzzle outputs
useCases.scenario: Predicting the output of Object.keys(), for..in, or similar enumeration.

useCases.scenario: Designing serializable records whose displayed keys have predictable ordering.

useCases.title: Selecting a collection
useCases.scenario: Choosing between an object and Map when insertion order is a core requirement.

interview.question: Are JavaScript object keys always returned in insertion order?
interview.answer: Object keys follow a special order: integer properties are sorted numerically, while other properties appear in creation order. Therefore, adding "2" after "100" can still make it appear first.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve straightforward insertion order for arbitrary key types? Use Map, whose entries iterate in insertion order.

interview.question: How can you inspect an object’s key order?
interview.answer: For own enumerable string keys, Object.keys() returns keys in the same ordering used by object enumeration. Numeric-looking keys therefore appear in ascending numeric order, followed by ordinary string keys.
interview.followUp: What does Object.getOwnPropertyNames() add? It also includes non-enumerable own string properties, while preserving the corresponding enumeration ordering.

interview.question: Does the rule apply identically to every kind of property key?
interview.answer: The documented object-key rule distinguishes integer properties from other properties. Only the non-integer string-key group follows creation order; symbols are a separate property-key category.
interview.followUp: What collection supports keys of any value and insertion-order iteration? Map supports arbitrary key values and remembers insertion order.

keyPoints: Object enumeration is ordered, but not by a single universal insertion-order rule.
Integer property names are emitted in ascending order; ordinary string properties use their creation order.
An object stores data as properties, each pairing a key with a value.
Object property keys are strings or symbols; values may have any type.
Known property names can be accessed with dot notation.
Bracket notation lets code compute or obtain the property name dynamically.
gotchas: An object does not use pure insertion order: integer properties are reordered numerically before ordinary string keys.

Object.freeze.summary: Object.freeze() prevents extensions and makes an object's existing properties non-writable and non-configurable. It returns the same object, while nested objects remain mutable unless frozen separately.
Object.freeze.explanation: Object.freeze marks an object as non-extensible and makes its existing data properties non-writable and non-configurable. It returns the same object rather than creating a copy; referenced nested objects remain independently mutable unless they are frozen too.

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: The object to freeze.

Object.freeze.returns: The object that was passed to the function.

example.explanation: The outer object is frozen, but freezing does not recursively freeze objects referenced by its properties.

useCases.scenario: Expose configuration objects that callers should not modify.

useCases.title: Stabilize shared data
useCases.scenario: Prevent accidental mutation of shared constants or state snapshots.

useCases.scenario: Lock an API object's shape and property descriptors before handing it to other code.

interview.question: What does Object.freeze do?
interview.answer: Object.freeze prevents extensions and sets existing data properties to non-writable and non-configurable. It also prevents changing the object's prototype. The method returns the same object it receives.
interview.followUp: Does it deep-freeze nested objects? No. A nested object must be passed to Object.freeze separately, typically through a deliberate recursive utility.

interview.question: What happens when code modifies a frozen object?
interview.answer: In strict mode, attempts to add, delete, or assign to restricted properties throw TypeError. In non-strict code, such operations can fail silently.
interview.followUp: Would a setter on a frozen object stop working? No. Accessor setters can still be invoked because freezing does not remove accessor behavior.

interview.question: Does Object.freeze create a copy?
interview.answer: Object.freeze returns the input object, not a new copy, so identity is preserved. Freezing also makes the object non-extensible and locks the relevant property descriptors.
interview.followUp: How does Object.freeze differ from Object.seal? Sealing prevents extensions and property deletion, while freezing additionally makes existing data properties immutable.

keyPoints: The operation first makes the object non-extensible, then tightens descriptors for its existing properties.
Existing data-property values cannot be reassigned after freezing.
A frozen object's prototype cannot be replaced.
Compared with sealing, freezing additionally prevents reassignment of existing data properties.
The return value is the exact input reference.
gotchas: Adding or removing properties, or changing frozen data properties, may fail silently in non-strict code but throws TypeError in strict code.
Freezing an accessor property does not freeze the value produced by its getter or prevent its setter from being called.
The method returns the original object, so assigning the result to another variable does not produce an independent frozen clone.
The operation is shallow: object-valued properties can still be changed unless those referenced objects are frozen separately.

Object.seal.summary: Object.seal(obj) prevents adding or removing properties and makes existing properties non-configurable. Writable existing values can still change.
Object.seal.explanation: Object.seal makes an object non-extensible and marks every existing property as non-configurable. The object keeps its current properties, so additions and removals are blocked, but existing data-property values may still change when writable.

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: The object to seal.

Object.seal.returns: The same object that was passed to the method.

example.explanation: Sealing keeps the existing property set fixed while still allowing writable property values to change.

useCases.title: Expose a stable mutable API shape
useCases.scenario: Prevent consumers from deleting or adding public fields without making every value immutable.

useCases.title: Constrain shared object structure
useCases.scenario: Apply a shallow structural restriction before passing an object across a module boundary.

interview.question: What does Object.seal do?
interview.answer: Object.seal prevents extensions and makes all existing properties non-configurable. Therefore, properties cannot be added or removed, but writable existing values can still be changed.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from Object.freeze()? Object.freeze also makes existing data properties non-writable, whereas Object.seal leaves writable values mutable.

interview.question: Does Object.seal return a new object?
interview.answer: The method returns the same object reference that it receives; it does not create a sealed copy. The object itself becomes non-extensible and its existing properties become non-configurable.
interview.followUp: How could you preserve the original object while sealing independently? Create a copy first, then pass that copy to Object.seal.

interview.question: How can code verify that an object is sealed?
interview.answer: A sealed object is non-extensible and has no configurable own properties. Object.isSealed can be used to test that state, returning true when those conditions hold.
interview.followUp: Is every non-extensible object sealed? No. Non-extensibility alone is insufficient; all existing properties must also be non-configurable.

keyPoints: The object's set of properties becomes fixed: later code cannot add new properties or remove existing ones.
Every property already present receives a non-configurable descriptor, preventing descriptor changes and deletion.
Sealing does not make writable data values immutable.
Sealing preserves the existing prototype chain, although the object's own [[Prototype]] cannot be reassigned because extensions are disabled.
The return value is the sealed input object, enabling direct assignment when useful.
gotchas: Adding or deleting properties fails; in strict mode, the failed operation normally throws a TypeError, while non-strict code may fail silently.
Sealing is weaker than freezing: writable existing values remain mutable.
Object.seal does not affect class private elements.

Operator precedence.summary: Operator precedence determines how JavaScript groups operators in an expression. Higher-precedence operators run before lower-precedence ones, while associativity handles operators at the same level.
Operator precedence.explanation: JavaScript uses operator precedence to group an expression. An operator with higher precedence is applied before one with lower precedence. Operators at the same precedence level use associativity. Parentheses create an explicit grouping and can change the result.

example.title: Precedence and parentheses
example.explanation: Multiplication runs before addition. Parentheses change the grouping, so the addition runs first.

useCases.scenario: Combine arithmetic operators in one expression.

useCases.title: Use parentheses for clarity
useCases.scenario: Make an expression's order clear to readers.

useCases.title: Read right-associative operators
useCases.scenario: Understand chained assignments and exponentiation.

interview.question: What is operator precedence?
interview.answer: Operator precedence decides which operators form groups first. Higher-precedence operators are grouped before lower-precedence operators; parentheses can override that grouping.
interview.followUp: What does `3 + 4 * 5` produce? It produces `23`, because multiplication is grouped before addition.

interview.question: What is associativity?
interview.answer: Associativity decides how operators with the same precedence are grouped. Left-associative operators group from left to right, while right-associative operators group from right to left.
interview.followUp: How is `a = b = 5` grouped? It is `a = (b = 5)`, because assignment is right-associative.

interview.question: How can code override operator precedence?
interview.answer: Parentheses create a grouped expression and can override the normal precedence rules. For example, `(3 + 4) * 5` evaluates addition before multiplication.
interview.followUp: Are operands evaluated according to precedence? No. Operands are evaluated from left to right; precedence controls operator grouping.

keyPoints: A higher-precedence operator is grouped before a lower-precedence operator.
Associativity controls grouping when operators have equal precedence.
Left-associative operators group their left operation first.
Right-associative operators group their right operation first.
Parentheses let you choose the intended grouping explicitly.
JavaScript evaluates operands from left to right, even when operator precedence differs.
gotchas: Precedence does not change the left-to-right evaluation order of operands.
Assignments group from right to left, so `a = b = 5` means `a = (b = 5)`.
Exponentiation runs before multiplication, division, addition, and other lower-precedence operators.

Optional Chaining.summary: Optional chaining (`?.`) safely accesses nested properties, computed properties, or methods when a value may be null or undefined. It short-circuits that chain and returns undefined instead of throwing.
Optional Chaining.explanation: Optional chaining safely accesses a property, computed property, or method when an earlier value may be null or undefined. It stops that continuous chain and returns undefined instead of throwing; a method call is skipped when the method is absent.
Optional Chaining.returns: undefined when the value before the optional chain is null or undefined; otherwise it produces the requested property value or call result.

example.title: Safe property and method access
example.code:
const user = { profile: { name: "Ada" } };

console.log(user.profile?.name); // "Ada"
console.log(user.settings?.theme); // undefined
console.log(user.profile?.["name"]); // "Ada"
console.log(user.notify?.("hello")); // undefined
example.explanation: Each optional chain continues only when the value before ?. is neither null nor undefined.

useCases.title: Nullable nested data
useCases.scenario: Read optional fields from API responses or configuration objects without manually checking every intermediate object.

useCases.title: Optional callbacks and methods
useCases.scenario: Invoke an optional callback or object method only when it exists.

useCases.title: Dynamic property names
useCases.scenario: Read a property whose key is computed at runtime while safely handling a missing base object.

interview.question: What does optional chaining do?
interview.answer: Optional chaining evaluates the left side and, if it is null or undefined, stops the chain and produces undefined. If the value exists, normal property access or invocation proceeds.
interview.followUp: What happens with `obj?.a.b` when `obj.a` is undefined? The chain does not protect `b`; use `obj?.a?.b` when both links may be absent.

interview.question: What are the main optional-chaining forms?
interview.answer: The documented forms are `obj?.prop`, `obj?.[prop]`, and `obj.method?.()`. They respectively guard property access, computed-property access, and calling a method that may not exist.
interview.followUp: How can you safely call a possibly absent function stored directly in `fn`? Use `fn?.()`; it returns undefined when `fn` is null or undefined.

interview.question: What is short-circuited besides the property access?
interview.answer: Optional chaining short-circuits evaluation, so an expression used as a computed property is not evaluated when the left value is null or undefined. The short circuit applies only to one continuous chain.
interview.followUp: Does grouping preserve the whole-chain short circuit? No: grouping ends the chain, so a later access can still throw if its grouped result is undefined.

keyPoints: Use repeated `?.` links to traverse nested data whose intermediate objects may be missing.
A nullish value immediately before `?.` ends the chain and yields undefined instead of causing the usual property-access error.
The syntax supports ordinary properties, bracket expressions, and optional method calls: `obj?.prop`, `obj?.[key]`, and `obj.method?.()`.
The root identifier must exist lexically; optional chaining handles a declared variable containing undefined, not an undeclared name.
Besides dot access, optional chaining can guard calls and computed property access.
gotchas: Optional chaining cannot rescue an undeclared identifier: `undeclared?.prop` still raises a ReferenceError. Declare the variable first, even if its value is undefined.
One `?.` protects only the immediately preceding value. Add another optional chain for each nullable link, such as `user?.address?.street`.
Because a missing value becomes undefined rather than an error, use this syntax only when absence is an acceptable result; otherwise validate required data explicitly.

parseInt radix.summary: parseInt() reads an integer from a string using a chosen number base. Give the radix explicitly when the base is known, and check for NaN when parsing can fail.
parseInt radix.explanation: The function converts its input to a string, ignores leading whitespace, and reads an integer from the start. The radix selects the number system, from base 2 through base 36. Reading stops when a character is not valid for that radix; if no valid digits are found, the result is NaN.

parameters.description: The value to parse; it is converted to a string, and leading whitespace is ignored.

parameters.name: radix
parameters.description: An optional integer from 2 to 36 that selects the number base. If omitted or 0, the default is normally base 10, with 0x or 0X input using base 16.

parseInt radix.returns: An integer parsed from the input. The result is NaN when the input does not start with a valid integer for the selected radix.

example.title: Parse integers with an explicit radix
example.explanation: The first call reads 101 as a base-2 number. The second call cannot find a valid integer.

useCases.scenario: Convert text containing a whole-number prefix, such as a value read from an input field.

useCases.title: Convert another number base
useCases.scenario: Decode values written in binary, hexadecimal, or another supported base.

useCases.title: Discard a decimal fraction
useCases.scenario: Extract the whole-number portion from a decimal string.

interview.question: What does parseInt() do?
interview.answer: parseInt() reads an integer from the start of a string and uses the supplied radix as its base. Leading whitespace is ignored, and the result is NaN when no valid integer can be read.
interview.followUp: What happens with parseInt("12px", 10)? It returns 12 because parsing stops when it reaches the first invalid character.

interview.question: Why should the radix usually be supplied?
interview.answer: The radix is an integer from 2 through 36. It tells parseInt() which digits are valid and how to calculate the result, so parseInt("101", 2) returns 5.
interview.followUp: What should code do when the radix is not known? Validate it before calling parseInt(), because values outside the documented range are invalid.

interview.question: How does parseInt() signal invalid input?
interview.answer: If no valid integer begins the input, the function returns NaN. Use Number.isNaN() to test that result when parsing may fail.
interview.followUp: Does parseInt("1.9", 10) return 2? No. It returns 1 because the fractional part is discarded.

keyPoints: parseInt() returns an integer interpreted in the chosen number base.
Spaces before the number do not affect the parsed result.
The radix must be an integer from 2 to 36.
Base 16 accepts letters such as f and converts "ff" to 255.
A hexadecimal prefix works when the radix is 16.
gotchas: Pass the radix explicitly when the base matters, especially for binary, octal, or hexadecimal input.

Pass by Reference.summary: JavaScript passes arguments by value, not by reference. For object arguments, the copied value still identifies the same object, so property mutations are visible to the caller while parameter reassignment is local.
Pass by Reference.explanation: JavaScript passes arguments by value. When that value identifies an object, both the caller and the parameter can refer to the same object, so property mutations are visible outside the function; reassigning the parameter only changes the local parameter binding.

example.title: Mutation versus parameter reassignment
example.explanation: Mutating the shared object is observable through the original variable, but assigning a new value to the parameter does not replace the caller's variable.

useCases.title: Intentional in-place updates
useCases.scenario: Update a mutable object in a function when the caller should observe the change.

useCases.title: Immutable transformations
useCases.scenario: Avoid changing shared state by returning a new object rather than mutating an argument.

interview.question: Does JavaScript pass objects by reference?
interview.answer: JavaScript arguments are passed by value. For an object, the copied value is an object reference, so changing a property affects the same object seen by the caller, while assigning a new object to the parameter does not change the caller's binding.
interview.followUp: What term more accurately describes object arguments? Object arguments are commonly described as passed by sharing: the reference value is copied, and both bindings can reach the same object.

interview.question: What happens when a function reassigns an object parameter?
interview.answer: No. If a function assigns `parameter = null` or `parameter = {}`, only its local parameter changes. The caller's variable still contains its original value.
interview.followUp: How can a function change the caller-visible object? It can mutate the object's existing properties, or explicitly return a replacement for the caller to assign.

interview.question: Why is `object.property = value` visible outside a function?
interview.answer: A property mutation operates on the shared object, so the caller observes it. Parameter reassignment changes only which value the local parameter refers to.
interview.followUp: What design choice avoids unintended mutation? Create and return a copy, then have the caller use the returned value instead of modifying the shared object.

keyPoints: Function calls copy argument values into parameters; JavaScript does not provide pass-by-reference parameters.
A parameter holding an object reference can mutate that object's properties, making the change observable to the caller.
Replacing the parameter's value does not replace the value stored in the caller's variable.
Property changes remain visible after the function returns because the parameter and caller reach the same object.
gotchas: Calling this pass by reference is misleading: reassigning a parameter never changes the caller's variable.
An object argument can expose mutations to its properties, even though the argument itself is still passed by value.

Promise resolution order.summary: Promise handlers are deferred to the microtask queue, even when a promise is already settled. They run after current synchronous code and in FIFO order, before the event loop advances to later macrotasks.
Promise resolution order.explanation: Promise handlers are never run immediately, even when their promises are already settled. They are queued as microtasks, and the engine runs queued handlers only after the current synchronous code finishes; a chained handler is queued when its preceding handler completes.

example.title: Promise handlers run through the microtask queue
example.explanation: Synchronous code runs first. Promise handlers then run in FIFO order; the nested handler is added after the existing second handler, so it runs last among these microtasks.

useCases.title: Debug asynchronous ordering
useCases.scenario: Predicting console output in code that mixes synchronous statements, promises, and timers.

useCases.title: Sequence promise chains
useCases.scenario: Ensuring dependent asynchronous steps execute only after earlier results settle.

useCases.title: Schedule microtasks
useCases.scenario: Deferring a small callback until the current call stack is clear without creating a timer.

interview.question: Why does Promise.resolve().then(handler) not call handler immediately?
interview.answer: Promise handlers are placed in the microtask queue and execute after the current JavaScript stack becomes empty. The queue is FIFO, so handlers already queued run before handlers added later.
interview.followUp: What happens if a microtask queues another microtask? The newly queued microtask runs after microtasks already waiting, but before the event loop proceeds to another macrotask.

interview.question: How are promise handlers ordered relative to setTimeout callbacks?
interview.answer: The synchronous part of the script runs first. After it finishes, the engine drains the microtask queue before processing timers or other macrotasks, so promise output appears before setTimeout output.
interview.followUp: Would rendering occur between two promise handlers? Normally no: the microtask queue is drained before rendering or another macrotask is processed.

interview.question: Why does each handler in a promise chain run in a separate asynchronous step?
interview.answer: In a chain, each then returns a new promise. A handler's returned value settles that new promise, allowing the next handler to be queued with that value once the preceding step completes.
interview.followUp: What if a handler returns a pending promise? The next handler waits until that returned promise settles, then receives its fulfillment value or rejection.

keyPoints: Promise-related microtasks execute in FIFO order.
A queued promise handler waits until the current synchronous execution has finished.
Settling a promise schedules its registered handlers instead of invoking them immediately.
Promise reactions consistently pass through the promise-jobs, or microtask, queue.
Handlers run only after the current synchronous code completes.
When several handlers are queued, earlier enqueued reactions precede later ones.
gotchas: An already-resolved promise does not make its handler synchronous; code after the registration runs first.
Each handler in a chain gets its own asynchronous turn rather than the whole chain executing as one synchronous operation.
A large or self-extending microtask queue can delay timers, rendering, and other event handling.

interview.question: What does Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors() return?
interview.answer: It returns an object whose keys are the source object's own property keys and whose values are property descriptor objects. The descriptors describe data properties or accessor properties.
interview.followUp: How can it help clone an object? Use Object.defineProperties with the returned descriptors, and separately preserve the prototype if needed.

interview.question: What fields can a property descriptor contain?
interview.answer: A data descriptor can contain value and writable. An accessor descriptor can contain get and set. Both kinds can contain configurable and enumerable.
interview.followUp: Can one descriptor contain both value and get? No. A property descriptor must describe either a data property or an accessor property.

interview.question: Why is this method useful for cloning?
interview.answer: It examines all own properties, including non-enumerable and symbol-keyed properties. This gives more complete information than ordinary property-copying loops.
interview.followUp: Why does Object.assign() differ? It copies enumerable own properties by reading their values, so it does not preserve descriptors.

The return value is a new object that maps property keys to descriptor records.
Property keys can be strings or Symbols, and each property has a descriptor.

Accessor descriptors can provide a getter function through get.

Prototype chain.explanation: When JavaScript reads a missing property, it checks the object's prototype, then that prototype's prototype, and continues until null. A property on the object itself wins over a property with the same name higher in the chain; this is called shadowing. Object.create() sets a prototype when creating an object, while Object.getPrototypeOf() reads it.

interview.question: How does a prototype chain resolve a property?
interview.answer: JavaScript looks for a property on the object first. If it is absent, it checks each prototype in order until it finds the property or reaches null.
interview.followUp: What happens when a property exists both on an object and its prototype? The object's own property is used, so it shadows the inherited property.

interview.question: How do you create and inspect a prototype relationship?
interview.answer: Object.create(proto) makes a new object whose prototype is proto. The new object can use properties and functions from proto without copying them.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the link? Use Object.getPrototypeOf(object), which returns the object's prototype.

interview.question: What is the role of a constructor's prototype?
interview.answer: A constructor's prototype becomes the prototype of objects created with new. Methods placed there can be shared by all those objects through the prototype chain.
interview.followUp: Why can long chains be costly? Missing-property lookups traverse the whole chain, and properties high in the chain may take longer to find.

keyPoints: Each object has a prototype object that supplies inherited properties.
The prototype chain stops at null.
Use Object.getPrototypeOf() to inspect a prototype.
An own property takes priority over an inherited property with the same name.
Object.create() creates an object with a chosen prototype.
For constructor functions, instances use the constructor's prototype object.
gotchas: Do not use __proto__ to change prototypes in new code. Prefer Object.setPrototypeOf().
Changing a prototype after object creation can hurt engine optimizations. Set it when creating the object when possible.

Prototype Chain.summary: JavaScript resolves missing properties by walking an object's prototype chain. The chain ends at null; if no object provides the property, the result is undefined.
Prototype Chain.explanation: Each object can link to another object as its prototype. When a property is missing on the object itself, JavaScript searches that prototype, then continues through successive prototypes until it finds the property or reaches null; a missing property evaluates to undefined.

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: The object whose prototype is returned.

Prototype Chain.returns: The prototype object associated with the supplied object.

example.title: Property lookup through a prototype chain
example.explanation: The child has no own greet method, so JavaScript finds it on parent through the prototype chain.

useCases.title: Method delegation
useCases.scenario: Share methods among related objects without copying each method onto every instance.

useCases.title: Prototype inspection
useCases.scenario: Inspect an object's inheritance relationship during debugging or metaprogramming.

useCases.title: Custom object composition
useCases.scenario: Create an object that delegates property lookup to a selected parent object.

interview.question: How does property lookup use the prototype chain?
interview.answer: JavaScript first checks whether the object has the requested property. If it does not, lookup continues on the object's prototype, then on that prototype's prototype, until the property is found or the chain ends; an unsuccessful lookup produces undefined.
interview.followUp: What terminates the search? The chain terminates at an object whose prototype is null.

interview.question: How can you inspect and create prototype relationships?
interview.answer: Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) returns the object's prototype. Object.create(proto) creates a new object whose prototype is the supplied object, allowing property lookup to delegate to it.
interview.followUp: How can the relationship be inspected without relying on __proto__? Use Object.getPrototypeOf, the standard access method described by the documentation.

interview.question: Where does the ordinary object prototype chain end?
interview.answer: Object.prototype is the default prototype for ordinary object literals, and its own prototype is null. Consequently, methods such as toString can be inherited through Object.prototype.
interview.followUp: Why does an array also find object methods? Its prototype chain eventually reaches Object.prototype, where those methods are available.

keyPoints: Property access checks own properties first and then searches the prototype.
Lookup continues through every successive prototype until a match or the chain's end.
A property absent from the entire chain evaluates to undefined.
Use Object.getPrototypeOf to inspect a prototype instead of treating __proto__ as the standard API.
Object.prototype is the terminal ordinary-object prototype because its prototype is null.
Object.create establishes a chosen prototype when creating an object.
gotchas: A prototype can have its own prototype, creating a chain rather than a single fallback object.
Prototype lookup eventually stops at null; it does not continue indefinitely.
Do not confuse an object's prototype link with the prototype property found on constructor functions.

Proxy traps.summary: JavaScript Proxy traps let a handler intercept fundamental operations on a target, such as property access, assignment, deletion, calls, and construction. Traps can customize behavior or delegate transparently to the target.
Proxy traps.explanation: A proxy handler can intercept fundamental operations on a target object through named traps. Each trap receives operation-specific arguments and can implement custom behavior or delegate to Reflect.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The original object or function whose operations may be intercepted.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: An object containing trap methods for selected operations.

parameters.name: property
parameters.description: The property key involved in a property operation.

parameters.name: receiver
parameters.description: The object used as the receiver for get and set operations.

Proxy traps.returns: A Proxy object that forwards unhandled operations to the target and applies the handler's traps where defined.

example.title: Intercepting object operations
example.explanation: The proxy validates assignments, hides a private-looking property, and filters it from key enumeration.

useCases.title: Validation
useCases.scenario: Reject or transform invalid assignments before they reach the target.

useCases.title: Logging and monitoring
useCases.scenario: Record reads, writes, calls, or other operations for diagnostics.

useCases.title: Access control
useCases.scenario: Expose a controlled interface while hiding selected properties or operations.

useCases.title: Function and constructor interception
useCases.scenario: Add behavior to callable or constructible objects without changing their original implementation.

interview.question: What is a JavaScript Proxy and what does a handler do?
interview.answer: A proxy wraps a target and uses a handler to intercept operations such as property reads, writes, deletion, calls, and construction. The handler can handle an operation itself or forward it to the target, commonly through Reflect.
interview.followUp: How can a proxy intercept a function call? Define an apply trap with signature apply(target, thisArg, args), or use a construct trap for new.

interview.question: Which arguments do get and set traps receive?
interview.answer: The get trap runs when a property is read and receives target, property, and receiver. The set trap runs when a property is assigned and receives target, property, value, and receiver; it should return a boolean indicating success.
interview.followUp: Why pass receiver to Reflect.get or Reflect.set? It preserves the proxy as the receiver, which matters for inherited accessors and prototype-based behavior.

interview.question: What restrictions apply to proxy traps?
interview.answer: A proxy cannot freely contradict certain target invariants. For example, a set trap cannot report success while changing a non-writable, non-configurable data property to a different value; violations can produce TypeError.
interview.followUp: What other trap can affect enumeration? ownKeys controls keys returned by operations such as Object.keys, while descriptor and configurability rules still constrain the result.

keyPoints: Create a proxy with a target and a handler; accesses through the proxy can be customized without modifying the target itself.
Use get and set to customize reads and assignments, including validation, logging, access control, or computed values.
The has trap handles membership checks made with the in operator.
The deleteProperty trap intercepts deletion attempts, including deletion of properties that do not exist.
A callable proxy can intercept invocation through apply, which receives the target function, this value, and argument list.
The construct trap customizes new operations, but the proxy target must itself be constructible.

Recursion limits.summary: JavaScript engines cap the number of nested recursive calls because each call uses stack space. The exact limit varies by engine, and exceeding it can raise a maximum-stack-size error.
Recursion limits.explanation: Each recursive call creates another execution context on the call stack, so deeper recursion consumes more memory. JavaScript engines impose a runtime-dependent maximum depth; exceeding it typically raises a stack-overflow error, making iteration preferable for very deep work.

example.title: Observing the runtime limit
example.explanation: This deliberately recurses until the runtime rejects another nested call; the reported depth varies by JavaScript engine, so it is for experimentation rather than production logic.

useCases.title: Measure an environment's practical limit
useCases.scenario: Testing runtime behavior across browsers or JavaScript hosts.

useCases.title: Prefer an explicit stack when depth may be large
useCases.scenario: Processing deeply nested trees or graphs.

useCases.title: Set and validate a safe maximum depth
useCases.scenario: Designing recursive algorithms with bounded input.

interview.question: What is recursion depth, and why is it limited?
interview.answer: Recursion depth is the maximum number of nested calls, counting the initial call. Each call adds an execution context to the stack, and the engine limits how many contexts can coexist.
interview.followUp: What determines the exact limit? The JavaScript engine and its available stack configuration; code should not depend on a particular numeric threshold.

interview.question: Why can deep recursion fail even when the algorithm is logically correct?
interview.answer: A recursive call creates another execution context, which consumes memory while callers wait to resume. Consequently, sufficiently deep recursion can exceed the stack and produce a maximum-stack-size error.
interview.followUp: How would you handle very deep input? Rewrite the algorithm iteratively, often using an explicit stack or another loop-based worklist.

interview.question: Does tail recursion remove JavaScript's recursion limit?
interview.answer: Tail-call optimization can avoid retaining the caller's execution context when the recursive call is the final operation. The documentation notes that support is not universal, so it cannot generally be relied on in JavaScript.
interview.followUp: Does putting the recursive call last guarantee safety? No; the running engine must implement the optimization, and most engines do not.

keyPoints: Recursion depth counts every active nested invocation, including the first function call.
For a recursive process whose deepest active chain contains n calls, the recursion depth is n.
The limit is imposed by the runtime engine rather than defined as one universal number for all JavaScript environments.
Active execution contexts consume memory, so increasing recursion depth increases the memory needed by the call stack.
Going beyond the available stack can result in a maximum-stack-size error.
Some engines can optimize a final recursive call so the current context need not remain on the stack.
gotchas: There is no single portable recursion limit: the maximum depth depends on the JavaScript engine.
Even a tail-position recursive call is not a safe way to assume unlimited depth, because most engines do not provide the relevant optimization.

Reflect methods.summary: Reflect exposes function-based forms of interceptable object operations, with method names matching Proxy traps. It is commonly used in proxy handlers to forward the default operation after adding custom behavior.
Reflect methods.explanation: Reflect provides function forms of JavaScript's interceptable object operations. Its methods correspond to Proxy traps, so a proxy handler can add behavior and then delegate the default operation to Reflect with the same arguments.
Reflect methods.returns: Individual Reflect methods return the result of their corresponding object operation; for example, Reflect.get returns a property value and Reflect.set returns a success boolean.

example.title: Forward proxy operations with Reflect
example.explanation: The proxy logs operations, while Reflect forwards each operation to the target using the trap's matching arguments.

useCases.title: Proxy forwarding
useCases.scenario: A proxy logs, validates, or measures property reads and writes before delegating normal behavior.

useCases.title: Dynamic object operations
useCases.scenario: Code needs property access, assignment, deletion, or construction through dynamically selected operations.

useCases.title: Default semantic delegation
useCases.scenario: A proxy handler must preserve ordinary JavaScript semantics instead of reimplementing inheritance and accessors.

interview.question: What is Reflect used for?
interview.answer: Reflect is a built-in object whose static methods invoke interceptable object internal methods. Each method corresponds to a Proxy handler method, such as Reflect.get for property reads and Reflect.set for writes.
interview.followUp: How can a proxy preserve normal behavior after logging a property read? The get trap should call Reflect.get with the target, property key, and receiver.

interview.question: How do Reflect.get() and Reflect.set() map to ordinary operations?
interview.answer: Reflect.get(target, key) performs a property read as a function call, while Reflect.set(target, key, value) performs an assignment-like operation. Reflect.set returns a boolean indicating whether the update succeeded.
interview.followUp: Why pass receiver to Reflect.get or Reflect.set? It preserves the receiver used by accessor lookup and assignment, which matters when inherited getters or setters are involved.

interview.question: What does Reflect.construct() do?
interview.answer: Reflect.construct(target, argumentsList) performs the constructor operation represented by new target(...argumentsList). Reflect.construct can also receive newTarget, allowing the constructed object's prototype relationship to use a different constructor.
interview.followUp: What does newTarget change? It changes the constructor's new.target value and can make the resulting object an instance of newTarget rather than target.

keyPoints: Reflect is especially useful inside proxy traps: it lets custom behavior delegate the underlying operation without manually reproducing it.
Reflect's static method names align with Proxy trap names, making the API predictable when forwarding operations.
Reflect.get(target, key) performs a property lookup and returns the resulting value.
Reflect.set(target, key, value[, receiver]) performs assignment and returns whether the update succeeded.
Reflect.construct(target, argumentsList) invokes a constructor with a dynamically supplied argument list.
gotchas: Reflect.set() reports assignment success with a boolean instead of exposing assignment syntax's result.
Reflect does not replace Proxy; it supplies the corresponding reflective operation used to forward a trap.
Reflect methods closely mirror low-level object operations, so they still perform the operation on the supplied target.

Regex lastIndex.summary: RegExp.lastIndex records where the next search starts for global and sticky regular expressions. Successful matches advance it, while failed exec() calls reset it to 0; assigning it manually selects a starting offset.
Regex lastIndex.explanation: A global or sticky RegExp stores the position used for its next search in lastIndex. A successful exec() or test() advances it to the end of the match; a failed search resets it to 0, and you can assign a starting position yourself.

example.title: Continuing and resetting a global match
example.explanation: A global regular expression resumes each exec() call at lastIndex; assigning 0 starts over.

useCases.title: Scanning successive matches
useCases.scenario: Iterate through every match while retaining capture groups and each match's position.

useCases.title: Resume from an offset
useCases.scenario: Start a global search at a known character offset.

useCases.title: Sticky tokenization
useCases.scenario: Parse input sequentially, requiring each token to begin exactly where the previous one ended.

interview.question: What does RegExp.lastIndex represent?
interview.answer: lastIndex is the position from which the next match begins for a global or sticky regular expression. After a successful exec(), it becomes the position immediately after the matched text; after failure, it resets to 0.
interview.followUp: What happens when lastIndex is beyond the input length? exec() finds no match and resets lastIndex to 0.

interview.question: How do global and sticky regexes differ when using lastIndex?
interview.answer: With g, the engine starts at lastIndex but may continue at later positions if the pattern does not match there. With y, matching must occur exactly at lastIndex, so it is useful for position-sensitive tokenization.
interview.followUp: How would you make a sticky regex parse from a chosen offset? Assign that offset to lastIndex before calling exec() or test().

interview.question: Why can repeated regex calls produce surprising results?
interview.answer: A global regex retains its position between calls, so repeated exec() calls can iterate through successive matches. The same stateful behavior applies to test(), which also advances lastIndex.
interview.followUp: How can a reused regex avoid stale state? Set lastIndex to 0 before the new search, or use suitable string methods that do not use the regex's saved position.

keyPoints: For a global regex, each subsequent exec() begins at the saved position and then advances that position after a match.
Assigning lastIndex lets you choose the offset where the next search begins.
The sticky flag requires the match to start exactly at lastIndex instead of scanning forward.
A failed search both returns null and resets the regular expression's saved position.
test() shares the stateful lastIndex behavior of exec() for global expressions.
String-based matching methods can avoid carrying state from an earlier regular-expression operation.
gotchas: Changing lastIndex has no effect on a regular expression without the global or sticky flag.
A failed exec() returns null and clears the saved position, so code must handle the failed result before reading the match.
Reusing a global regex can make later searches begin in the middle of a string; reset lastIndex when an independent search should start at the beginning.

requestAnimationFrame.summary: requestAnimationFrame schedules an animation callback for the browser's next suitable animation opportunity. The callback receives elapsed time in milliseconds, and its returned request ID can be used to cancel the scheduled call.
requestAnimationFrame.explanation: Calling requestAnimationFrame schedules a callback for the browser's next suitable animation-and-repaint opportunity. The callback receives elapsed page-load time in milliseconds; use that timestamp to calculate motion, and call requestAnimationFrame again when another frame is needed.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: The function scheduled to run when the browser is ready for the animation opportunity; it receives elapsed page-load time in milliseconds.

requestAnimationFrame.returns: A request identifier that can be passed to cancelAnimationFrame(requestId).

example.title: Animate an element with a frame loop
example.explanation: Moves the element for one second, using the callback timestamp to calculate progress and scheduling each next frame explicitly.

useCases.title: Custom element animation
useCases.scenario: Animating DOM properties that CSS cannot handle conveniently.

useCases.title: Time-based animation
useCases.scenario: Driving a visual update loop whose progress depends on elapsed time.

useCases.title: Cancellable animation
useCases.scenario: Stopping a pending animation when it is no longer needed.

interview.question: What does requestAnimationFrame do?
interview.answer: requestAnimationFrame schedules a callback for the nearest time when the browser wants to perform animation, typically while preparing a repaint. This lets the browser coordinate JavaScript animation work with rendering.
interview.followUp: How does a continuous animation continue? The callback must schedule the next frame by calling requestAnimationFrame again, usually after updating the element.

interview.question: What argument does the callback receive?
interview.answer: The callback receives one argument: the time elapsed since page loading, measured in milliseconds. This value can also be obtained with performance.now(), so it can drive time-based progress rather than assuming a fixed frame interval.
interview.followUp: Why use the supplied time? Frame timing depends on the browser, so elapsed time keeps motion consistent when frame intervals vary.

interview.question: How can a scheduled callback be cancelled?
interview.answer: The function returns a request ID. Pass that ID to cancelAnimationFrame(requestId) to cancel the scheduled callback before it runs.
interview.followUp: When is this useful? It allows an animation to stop cleanly when its target is removed, hidden, or no longer relevant.

keyPoints: The call accepts a callback and returns an identifier for the scheduled request.
The browser chooses the suitable execution moment rather than the code forcing an exact delay.
Use the callback's millisecond timestamp to calculate animation progress.
performance.now() provides the same kind of elapsed-time reference when independently measuring animation timing.
Use this API for animations that require JavaScript control or cannot be handled effectively by CSS.
gotchas: A scheduled callback runs once; keep its returned request ID if you may need to cancel it with cancelAnimationFrame.
DOM changes made in the callback can be grouped with other animation callbacks and CSS animations, reducing repeated geometry recalculation and repaint.

rest parameters.summary: Rest parameters let a function accept any number of arguments by collecting extras into an array. Spread syntax uses the same three dots to expand an iterable into separate arguments or values.
rest parameters.explanation: A rest parameter starts with `...` in a function declaration and collects all remaining arguments into a real array. Spread syntax also uses `...`, but in a function call or similar expression it expands an iterable, such as an array, into separate values.

parameters.name: named parameters
parameters.description: Named parameters before the rest parameter receive arguments by position.

parameters.name: ...rest
parameters.description: The final rest parameter receives all remaining arguments in a new array.

rest parameters.returns: A rest parameter itself does not define a return value; the containing function returns whatever its body returns.

example.title: Gather and expand arguments
example.explanation: The function keeps the first argument in `first` and gathers later arguments into the `rest` array. The spread syntax then expands an array into separate function arguments.

useCases.title: Variable-argument functions
useCases.scenario: A utility needs to accept any number of values.

useCases.title: Array operations on arguments
useCases.scenario: A function needs to process extra values with `map`, `reduce`, or `sort`.

useCases.title: Calling list-based APIs
useCases.scenario: An array must be passed to a function that expects separate arguments.

interview.question: What does a rest parameter do?
interview.answer: A rest parameter collects the remaining arguments into an array. It must be the final parameter, so `function f(a, ...rest)` stores all arguments after `a` in `rest`.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from `arguments`? `arguments` is array-like and includes every argument, while the rest value is a normal array containing only the remaining arguments.

interview.question: What is the difference between rest and spread syntax?
interview.answer: Spread syntax expands an iterable into separate values. For example, `Math.max(...numbers)` passes each array element as an individual argument instead of passing the array itself.
interview.followUp: Can spread be used with objects? Yes. Object spread creates a shallow copy or combines enumerable properties, but nested objects are still shared.

interview.question: Why prefer rest parameters over `arguments`?
interview.answer: Rest parameters are real arrays, so array methods such as `sort`, `map`, and `reduce` can be called directly on them. The older `arguments` object does not support those array methods.
interview.followUp: What happens when no extra arguments are supplied? The rest parameter is an empty array, so its `length` is `0`.

keyPoints: In a function definition, `...name` gathers the arguments not matched by earlier named parameters into an array.
In a function call, `...value` expands an iterable into separate arguments.
The rest array is created from the extra arguments. Later changes to earlier named parameters do not change that array.
A rest parameter does not increase the function's `length` property.
The collected rest value can use destructuring patterns, which can skip selected positions.
gotchas: A function can have only one rest parameter, and it must be last. A trailing comma and a default value after `...rest` are not allowed.
`arguments` contains every argument, but it does not provide normal array methods such as `map()` or `sort()`. Rest parameters create a real array.
An arrow function has no own `arguments` object. If it uses `arguments`, the value comes from the surrounding normal function.

Set uniqueness.summary: A Set is a collection of values without keys where each value appears at most once. It is useful for membership checks and removing duplicates.
Set uniqueness.explanation: A Set stores values without keys and enforces uniqueness: adding a value already present has no effect. It can be initialized from an iterable, queried with has(), and converted back to an array when needed; iteration follows insertion order.

parameters.description: An optional iterable whose values are copied into the new Set.

Set uniqueness.returns: A Set object containing unique values from the optional iterable.

example.explanation: Constructing a Set from an iterable keeps each value only once, so spreading it back into an array removes duplicates.

useCases.title: Fast membership tracking
useCases.scenario: Track whether identifiers, permissions, or tags have already been seen.

useCases.title: Enforce uniqueness
useCases.scenario: Maintain a collection that must not contain repeated entries.

interview.question: What is the defining property of a Set?
interview.answer: A Set is a collection of values rather than key-value pairs, and each value can occur only once. It is useful when membership and uniqueness matter more than indexed access.
interview.followUp: How can an array be deduplicated? Construct a Set from the array and spread or convert that Set back into an array.

interview.question: How does new Set(iterable) initialize a Set?
interview.answer: The constructor accepts an iterable, commonly an array, and adds its elements to the new Set. Duplicate elements are therefore retained only once.
interview.followUp: What happens if no iterable is supplied? The constructor creates an empty Set.

interview.question: In what order are Set values iterated?
interview.answer: A Set can be traversed with for...of or forEach(), and its values are visited in insertion order. This preserves the order in which distinct values were successfully added.
interview.followUp: Which operation checks membership without modifying the collection? Use set.has(value), which returns a boolean.

keyPoints: Set is designed for collections of unique values and does not associate each value with a separate key.
Pass an iterable to the constructor to populate a Set immediately; an array is a common source.
Use has(value) for a boolean membership test without changing the Set.
clear() empties the entire collection in one operation.
The size property gives the number of values currently held by the Set.

interview.question: What is the difference between setTimeout and setInterval?
interview.answer: setTimeout schedules a function for one later call after the delay expires. setInterval schedules repeated calls using the interval.
interview.followUp: How can a repeating timer be stopped? Pass the identifier returned by setInterval to clearInterval.

interview.question: What arguments does setTimeout accept?
interview.answer: The function is the work to run, and the delay is the time in milliseconds before the timer expires. Extra arguments can be passed after the delay and are given to the function.
interview.followUp: What should be used instead of a string of code? Pass a function, not a string, to avoid dynamic code execution.

interview.question: How do you cancel a timeout?

interview.followUp: How is an interval cancelled? Use clearInterval with the identifier returned by setInterval.

setInterval starts after its delay and then keeps calling the function at that interval.
A timer can receive additional arguments after the delay; these arguments are passed to the callback.
The delay is optional in the documented setTimeout forms.

setTimeout runs only once. Use setInterval when the task must repeat.

Short Circuit Evaluation.summary: Short-circuit evaluation makes JavaScript stop evaluating a logical expression as soon as its result is determined. The || operator stops at a truthy value, while && stops at a falsy value, and each returns the operand where it stopped.
Short Circuit Evaluation.explanation: JavaScript evaluates logical operators from left to right. With ||, evaluation stops at the first truthy value; with &&, it stops at the first falsy value. The operator returns the operand where evaluation stopped, so the result does not have to be a Boolean.
Short Circuit Evaluation.returns: The operand at which evaluation stops; with || this is the first truthy value or the last operand, and with && it is the first falsy value or the last operand.

example.title: Short-circuiting with || and &&
example.explanation: The right side of each logical expression runs only when the left side cannot determine the result.

useCases.scenario: Choose a fallback when a value may be falsy.

useCases.title: Conditional execution with &&
useCases.scenario: Run an action only when a condition is truthy.

useCases.title: Guarding work
useCases.scenario: Avoid evaluating unnecessary expressions or side effects.

interview.question: How does short-circuit evaluation work for || and &&?
interview.answer: The operands are evaluated from left to right. For ||, JavaScript returns immediately when it finds a truthy operand; for &&, it returns immediately when it finds a falsy operand.
interview.followUp: What does `0 || 42` return? It returns 42, because 0 is falsy and evaluation continues to the right operand.

interview.question: Do logical operators always return Booleans?
interview.answer: Logical operators return one of their operands rather than converting the result to true or false. Thus, `"hello" || "fallback"` returns `"hello"`, while `"" || "fallback"` returns `"fallback"`.
interview.followUp: How can a Boolean result be forced? Apply Boolean conversion, such as `Boolean(value)`, or use `!!value`.

interview.question: Why can short-circuiting be useful beyond choosing a value?
interview.answer: The right operand is skipped when the left operand already determines the result. This makes expressions such as `condition && action()` useful for conditional execution, because `action()` runs only when `condition` is truthy.
interview.followUp: What happens with `a || b && c`? && has higher precedence, so it is grouped as `a || (b && c)`; parentheses can make that grouping explicit.

keyPoints: The || operator evaluates operands until it encounters a truthy value, then stops.
When every earlier operand is falsy, the final operand becomes the returned value.
An expression on the right of || is skipped when the left side is truthy.
gotchas: The ! operator binds more tightly than && and ||; use parentheses when combining operators if the intended grouping is not obvious.
A function call on the right side of || or && may never happen, so side effects must not be required unconditionally.

Spread vs Rest.summary: Rest parameters gather remaining function arguments into an array, while spread syntax expands an iterable into separate arguments or elements. Both use `...`, but their syntactic position determines which behavior applies.
Spread vs Rest.explanation: The same three-dot notation has opposite roles depending on where it appears: in a function parameter list, rest gathers remaining arguments into an array; in a call or similar expression, spread expands an iterable into separate arguments or elements.

useCases.scenario: Values from an iterable need to be inserted into an array or combined with other literal elements.

interview.question: How do rest parameters differ from spread syntax?
interview.answer: Rest parameters appear in a function definition and collect all remaining arguments into an array. Spread syntax appears in a call or similar expression and expands an iterable into separate arguments or elements.
interview.followUp: What happens if a rest parameter is followed by another parameter? It is invalid because the rest parameter must be last.

interview.question: Why use a rest parameter?
interview.answer: A rest parameter lets one function accept any number of arguments while providing those extra values as a real array. This is more convenient for array operations than an array-like argument collection.
interview.followUp: How would you pass the collected values to another function expecting separate arguments? Use spread syntax at the call site, such as `target(...values)`.

interview.question: How can an array be passed to a function that expects separate arguments?
interview.answer: Spread syntax expands an iterable in a function call, so an array can supply individual arguments to a function such as `Math.max`. The same notation can also expand values into array or object literals as documented on the page.
interview.followUp: What determines whether `...` gathers or expands? Its syntactic position: parameter-list position means rest, while call or similar expression position means spread.

keyPoints: A function parameter prefixed with `...` gathers the remaining supplied arguments into an array.
Rest is a collecting operation: values not assigned to earlier parameters are placed into one array.
Rest and spread share notation but perform inverse operations, so their position in the syntax determines the meaning.
Inside a function declaration's parameter list, trailing `...name` identifies a rest parameter.
At a call site, spread supplies the iterable's items as separate argument positions.
Rest parameters are useful for variadic functions whose callers may provide different argument counts.
gotchas: A rest parameter cannot precede another parameter; it must be the final parameter in the function definition.
Spread in a function call requires an iterable value, such as an array; it does not mean that every object can be expanded there.

Stack vs Heap.summary: JavaScript runs through an engine together with a host environment. The engine implements the language, while the host adds platform-specific features and access to the outside world.
Stack vs Heap.explanation: JavaScript uses an execution context to track the state needed while code runs. The engine manages a stack of active contexts, while objects and functions are stored in memory managed by the engine. The host environment supplies features outside the core language, such as timers or input and output. The exact runtime behavior depends on the host.

example.title: A function call creates an execution context
example.explanation: The object is stored in memory, and the function call creates an execution context for running its body.

useCases.title: Separate language from platform APIs
useCases.scenario: Explaining why browser APIs are not part of the JavaScript language itself.

useCases.title: Understand running code
useCases.scenario: Reasoning about what happens when a function is called.

useCases.title: Compare host environments
useCases.scenario: Comparing JavaScript behavior across browsers and runtimes.

interview.question: What is an execution context?
interview.answer: An execution context contains the state needed to run JavaScript code. The execution context stack tracks which context is currently running and returns to the previous one when a call finishes.
interview.followUp: How does an asynchronous callback fit this model? The host schedules work, and the callback runs later in a new execution context when the host allows it to run.

interview.question: What is the difference between the JavaScript engine and the host environment?
interview.answer: The JavaScript engine implements the ECMAScript language. The host environment adds mechanisms that let code interact with external resources and the surrounding platform.
interview.followUp: Why can the same JavaScript code behave differently in a browser and another runtime? The host-provided APIs and scheduling behavior can differ even when the language engine follows the same ECMAScript rules.

interview.question: Does the execution model describe the engine's physical implementation?
interview.answer: The abstract model describes language semantics, but implementations can optimize it. Therefore, the conceptual stack and memory model should not be treated as a promise about physical machine structures.
interview.followUp: Can engine optimization change the language result? It may change internal representation and execution strategy, but it must preserve the specified observable behavior.

keyPoints: The JavaScript engine parses JavaScript source code and executes it according to the language rules.
Running JavaScript involves both the language engine and the environment that embeds it.
The engine turns source text into an executable form and runs it.
Host mechanisms let JavaScript communicate with resources outside the language itself.
gotchas: The execution model is a specification model, not a complete description of how every browser or runtime implements JavaScript.
Do not assume that the abstract model maps directly to physical memory or internal engine data structures.
JavaScript alone does not provide every external capability; the host environment supplies environment-specific mechanisms.

Strict Mode.summary: Strict mode is a restricted form of JavaScript with different syntax and runtime behavior. Enable it with "use strict" at the start of a script or function; modules and classes enable it automatically.
Strict Mode.explanation: Strict mode is a restricted form of JavaScript that changes some syntax and runtime behavior. Add the exact directive at the start of a script or simple-parameter function; modules and class bodies use strict mode automatically.

example.title: Enable strict mode
example.explanation: The directive enables strict mode for the script. The function keeps the exact this value, and the undeclared assignment throws an error.

useCases.title: Check classic scripts
useCases.scenario: Use it in a classic script to detect mistakes such as undeclared assignments early.

useCases.title: Limit the scope
useCases.scenario: Use it in one function when only that function should use strict semantics.

useCases.title: Use modern code structures
useCases.scenario: Use modules or classes when you want strict behavior without adding the directive.

interview.question: How do you enable strict mode?
interview.answer: Use the exact statement "use strict"; before other statements in a script or function body. A script directive affects the script, while a function directive affects only that function.
interview.followUp: How do modules differ? Module contents are strict automatically, so no directive is needed.

interview.question: What behavior changes in strict mode?
interview.answer: Strict mode turns several silent failures into errors. Examples include assigning to an undeclared variable, writing to a non-writable property, and deleting an undeletable property.
interview.followUp: What happens with a failed assignment to a non-extensible object? Strict mode throws a TypeError instead of ignoring the assignment.

interview.question: How does strict mode affect this and arguments?
interview.answer: In strict mode, a function's this value is not replaced with the global object or boxed when called with null, undefined, or a primitive. The arguments object also does not stay synchronized with named parameters.
interview.followUp: What happens when a strict function changes a parameter? Its corresponding arguments entry keeps the original argument value.

keyPoints: It is an opt-in language mode, not merely a smaller set of JavaScript features.
You can enable it gradually because strict and non-strict code may exist in the same program.
Use the directive at the beginning of a script to apply strict mode to that whole script.
The with statement is not allowed because it makes variable lookup unpredictable.
Variables declared by strict eval stay inside the evaluated code and do not leak outward.
A strict function cannot declare two parameters with the same name.
gotchas: Put the directive before other statements. Code before it means it will not enable strict mode for the whole script.
A function with default, rest, or destructured parameters cannot contain this directive; doing so is a syntax error.
Placing the directive inside an ordinary block does not enable strict mode for that block.
Modules do not need the directive, and class bodies are strict automatically as well.

String coercion.summary: String coercion converts a value to text when JavaScript needs its string form. It happens implicitly in suitable operations or explicitly with String(value).
String coercion.explanation: JavaScript converts a value to text when an operation needs a string, such as displaying it. This conversion can happen implicitly, or explicitly with String(value). Common values receive predictable textual forms: booleans become "true" or "false", null becomes "null", and numbers become their textual representation.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value whose textual representation is required.

String coercion.returns: A string representation of the supplied value.

example.title: Explicit and implicit string conversion
example.code:
let value = true;
console.log(String(value)); // "true"
console.log(String(null));  // "null"
console.log("" + 1 + 2);   // "12"
example.explanation: Use String(value) when an explicit string conversion is intended; concatenation can produce different results because + handles strings and numbers differently.

useCases.scenario: Displaying a value through an API or output operation that requires text.

useCases.title: Explicit normalization
useCases.scenario: Making the conversion intent explicit before storing or passing textual data.

useCases.title: User-facing messages
useCases.scenario: Converting booleans or null into predictable text for labels or messages.

interview.question: When does string coercion occur, and how can it be requested explicitly?
interview.answer: String coercion occurs when JavaScript needs the string form of a value, such as while displaying it. It can also be requested explicitly with String(value).
interview.followUp: What does String(false) return? It returns the string "false", not the boolean false.

interview.question: What are the results of converting a boolean and null to strings?
interview.answer: String(true) produces "true", and String(null) produces "null". The result is a string even though the inputs have different types.
interview.followUp: How would you verify the result type? Apply typeof to the converted value; it returns "string".

interview.question: Why should explicit String(value) be preferred when text is required?
interview.answer: String conversion is distinct from numeric conversion: String(value) creates textual output, whereas arithmetic operators may convert operands to numbers. Use String when the required result is a string.
interview.followUp: What happens when a string is passed to Number instead? A numeric string can become a number, while an invalid numeric string becomes NaN.

keyPoints: Operators and functions may perform implicit conversion when their required input type differs from the supplied value.
String coercion supplies a value's textual representation when an operation needs text.
Use String(value) for an explicit conversion instead of relying on an operation to infer the desired type.
Boolean false and null convert to the literal strings "false" and "null".
String conversion is one of JavaScript's three commonly used type conversions, alongside number and boolean conversion.
gotchas: String conversion does not produce an empty string for null or booleans: null becomes "null", while false becomes "false".

String immutability.sourceTitle: JavaScript data types and data structures
String immutability.summary: JavaScript strings are immutable: once created, their contents cannot be changed. String operations return new strings, so retain the result when you need transformed text.
String immutability.explanation: A JavaScript string cannot be changed after it is created. Operations that appear to edit text instead produce another string, which you can store by assigning the returned value to a variable; the variable itself may still be reassigned.
String immutability.returns: String operations that transform or combine text return a new string; the original remains unchanged.

example.explanation: replace() returns a new string, so the original value remains unchanged.
